catalog_quote: Various analyses of Pijin have provided different accounts of the stress pattern of Pijin words. Bugotu (1972, p.27) says “Stress in Pidgin English, as is true in most Melanesian native tongues, usually falls on the penultimate syllable.” The account by Simons and Young (1978, p.18) says that “stress normally falls on the first syllable of Pijin words (although there are, of course, a few exceptions).” In saying that, they allow that epenthetic vowels in consonant clusters do not cause stress to shift to any new first syllable created by epenthesis. It seems that both positions express part of the truth. This is accounted for in Jourdan’s explanation of stress placement, namely that “word stress is lexically determined, and is retained on the original syllable of the etymon, regardless of what language the word is derived from, and regardless of where on the word the stress appears” (Jourdan & Selbach 2004, p.708). Of course for words that occur neither in the substrate vernaculars nor in English (e.g. yufala ‘you PL’) the only part of this account that is relevant is that stress is lexically determined. In conclusion, stress is not predictable, and the stressed syllable will retain the stress even when processes of epenthesis or word final vowel paragoge occur. While stress is lexically determined, there are no instances in which stress placement creates a contrast between words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Pijin is lexically fixed per word: each word keeps stress on the syllable that bore it in the source-language etymon (English or a Solomons vernacular), so there is no positional rule; stress stays on that syllable even when epenthetic vowels break clusters (klaem ~ kalaem) or a final vowel is added (skul ~ sukulu). Stress is never contrastive. Beimers explicitly rejects both the earlier fixed-penultimate (Bugotu 1972:27) and fixed: initial syllable (Simons & Young 1978:18) accounts as partial truths.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for simple words. Compounds: 'the stress falls on only one syllable of the compound words (usually the first syllable)' (p. 98-99); Simons & Young 1978:22 (as reported p. 122) put stress on the second syllable of reduplicated forms.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with no English or vernacular etymon (e.g. yufala) — stress simply lexical. Earlier sources' 'exceptions' to initial stress noted. Focus particles nao/ya receive higher pitch and 'phrase stress' (p. 56, p. ~172) — a phrase-level phenomenon, not word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (§3.9.2.2), explicitly distinguished from sentence intonation and focus-particle pitch (§3.9.2.3). The 1979 Peace Corps handbook only describes sentence intonation (peak 'on the last stressed syllable').
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Solomon Islands Pijin as a whole (piji1239), noting heavy inter-speaker variation (substrate-influenced epenthesis/paragoge) and, for stress, that lexical stress is retained across that variation. Beimers's title uses 'Solomon Islands Pidgin'; local name Pijin. No dialect specified.

sources.note: §3.9.2.2 Stress, p. 55: reviews Bugotu 1972 (penultimate) and Simons & Young 1978 (first syllable), adopts Jourdan & Selbach 2004:708 — word stress is lexically determined, retained on the etymon's original syllable regardless of source language; not predictable, survives epenthesis/paragoge, never contrastive. Also p. 122: Simons & Young say stress on 2nd syllable of reduplicated words; pp. 98-99: compounds carry one stress, usually on the first syllable; §3.9.2.3 focus particles nao/ya take higher pitch.
